front: What makes a slow pulse sinus bradycardia on ECG?
back: Sinus P waves precede each QRS with consistent atrioventricular conduction, at a slow rate.
explanation: Rate alone cannot determine the pacemaker origin; inspect the P waves and their relationship to QRS complexes.

front: Which findings make bradycardia clinically unstable?
back: Hypotension, shock, acute altered mental status, ischemic discomfort or acute heart failure attributable to the slow rhythm.
explanation: Treat the patient's perfusion and symptoms rather than applying an intervention solely because of a numerical heart rate.

front: What can bridge unstable bradycardia that is unresponsive to atropine?
back: Transcutaneous pacing or a rate-accelerating epinephrine or dopamine infusion, with expert help.
explanation: Persistent instability may require temporary transvenous pacing; supportive treatment continues while arranging it.

front: Which medication classes commonly cause sinus bradycardia?
back: Beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are important examples.
explanation: A medication history can identify reversible nodal suppression; drug effects must be considered before permanent pacing decisions.

front: Which endocrine disorder can cause sinus bradycardia with cold intolerance?
back: Hypothyroidism.
explanation: Recognizing associated systemic findings helps distinguish a reversible extrinsic cause from intrinsic sinus-node disease.

front: Does isolated nocturnal sinus bradycardia automatically require a pacemaker?
back: No; evaluate sleep apnea and other causes in context.
explanation: The timing and symptom relationship matter, and treatment of sleep-disordered breathing can improve nocturnal rhythm disturbances.

front: Why is symptom-rhythm correlation important in sinus-node dysfunction?
back: It helps show that the slow rhythm or pauses actually cause the patient's symptoms.
explanation: An asymptomatic office tracing may miss intermittent events or reveal an incidental resting rate.

front: Why must P-wave frequency be counted when evaluating a slow ventricular rate?
back: A normal atrial rate with blocked P waves indicates AV block rather than simple sinus slowing.
explanation: A slow pulse can reflect failure of impulse formation or failure of conduction; management depends on the mechanism.

front: How can a vasovagal episode slow the heart?
back: Transient parasympathetic activation reduces sinus-node firing.
explanation: Associated vasodilation can also lower blood pressure, so syncope is not explained by heart rate alone.

front: What is chronotropic incompetence?
back: Failure to increase heart rate appropriately with physiologic demand.
explanation: It can cause exertional intolerance even without profound resting bradycardia and requires clinical assessment.

front: What ECG pattern typically identifies a PVC?
back: An early, wide QRS without a preceding sinus P wave, often with discordant repolarization.
explanation: Ventricular activation begins outside the usual rapid conduction pathway, widening the complex.

front: Why can a PVC be perceived as a skipped beat followed by a thump?
back: The early beat may eject weakly, while the following post-pause beat is stronger.
explanation: Patients often notice the recovery beat more than the premature contraction itself.

front: What is a pulse deficit during frequent PVCs?
back: The ECG rate exceeds the palpable pulse rate because some ectopic beats have inadequate stroke volume.
explanation: Assess the patient and mechanical perfusion rather than relying on the monitor number alone.

front: What does PVC burden measure?
back: The proportion of recorded heartbeats that are PVCs.
explanation: Ambulatory monitoring is useful because a short ECG can underrepresent or overrepresent daily ectopy.

front: Why assess ventricular function in a patient with frequent PVCs?
back: A substantial burden can cause or worsen cardiomyopathy.
explanation: There is no single threshold proving causation; assess burden, competing causes and response to treatment.

front: What is the purpose of echocardiography when evaluating frequent PVCs?
back: To identify structural heart disease and assess ventricular function.
explanation: The same ECG ectopy can have different implications in a normal heart and a diseased heart.

front: Which electrolyte deficiencies can promote ventricular ectopy?
back: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.
explanation: Look for losses and medication effects; restoring electrolytes addresses a reversible arrhythmogenic influence.

front: Which accompanying features make PVCs more concerning?
back: Syncope, relevant family history, structural abnormalities or complex ectopy that increases with exercise.
explanation: Risk assessment depends on the clinical context and morphology, not just whether a PVC is present.

front: What is ventricular bigeminy?
back: Alternation of a normal beat and a PVC.
explanation: It describes the pattern, not by itself the cause or the patient's hemodynamic stability.

front: Can occasional PVCs be managed conservatively?
back: Yes, after assessing symptoms, burden and underlying cardiac disease.
explanation: Reassurance is most useful when grounded in an appropriate evaluation rather than a blanket claim that all ectopy is harmless.

front: What is the principal purpose of preoxygenation before RSI?
back: To increase oxygen reserves and delay desaturation during apnea.
explanation: A satisfactory initial saturation does not mean the patient has a large reserve, especially with severe lung disease.

front: Which preoxygenation approach may help a severely hypoxemic patient before RSI?
back: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation when feasible and appropriate.
explanation: Positive pressure can recruit lung units and improve the oxygen reserve before apnea.

front: Does a neuromuscular blocker provide sedation or analgesia?
back: No.
explanation: A paralyzed patient may remain conscious unless appropriate induction and continuing sedation/analgesia are provided.

front: Why can succinylcholine be dangerous after the acute phase of major burns or denervation?
back: It can trigger severe hyperkalemia.
explanation: Upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors increase potassium release during depolarization.

front: When should an awake intubation strategy be considered?
back: When difficult intubation is anticipated together with difficult ventilation, poor apnea tolerance, aspiration risk or difficult invasive rescue.
explanation: The airway plan should preserve safety before induction removes spontaneous breathing.

front: Why assess hemodynamic risk before RSI?
back: Induction and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate hypotension in a patient with limited reserve.
explanation: Resuscitation, drug selection and a plan for cardiovascular deterioration should accompany the airway plan.

front: Should corticosteroids routinely follow etomidate solely to counter adrenal suppression?
back: No.
explanation: A separate clinical indication for steroids must be considered independently from the induction drug choice.

front: What objective method should confirm and monitor tracheal tube placement?
back: Sustained waveform capnography, interpreted with the clinical examination.
explanation: A fleeting carbon dioxide signal or tube mist is insufficient; continued monitoring can detect displacement.

front: Why must post-intubation sedation be planned before RSI?
back: The induction drug can wear off while paralysis persists.
explanation: An immobile patient can still experience awareness and pain; reassessment and ongoing care are essential.

front: What takes priority after a failed intubation attempt with desaturation?
back: Restoring oxygenation.
explanation: Use the prepared rescue strategy, limit repeated traumatic attempts and escalate early when oxygenation cannot be maintained.

front: What is the defining ECG clue of a PAC?
back: An early P wave arising outside the sinus node, usually with a different morphology.
explanation: The QRS is often narrow if ventricular conduction proceeds normally.

front: How can a blocked PAC mimic a pause?
back: An early atrial impulse is not conducted through the refractory AV node.
explanation: Look for a premature P wave superimposed on the preceding T wave before diagnosing sinus arrest.

front: Can a PAC produce a wide QRS?
back: Yes, through aberrant intraventricular conduction.
explanation: An early abnormal P wave and the timing of the beat help distinguish an aberrantly conducted PAC from a PVC.

front: Why use ambulatory ECG monitoring for suspected PACs?
back: To capture intermittent beats and correlate them with symptoms.
explanation: A normal brief office tracing does not exclude episodic atrial ectopy.

front: Do isolated low-risk PACs necessarily need antiarrhythmic treatment?
back: No.
explanation: Management depends on symptoms and associated disease; reassurance can be sufficient after appropriate assessment.

front: Does a PAC diagnosis equal atrial fibrillation?
back: No.
explanation: Frequent PACs may warrant assessment for associated atrial disease or future arrhythmia, but they are not equivalent to documented AF.

front: What can different PAC P-wave morphologies indicate?
back: Multiple ectopic atrial origins.
explanation: P-wave shape reflects the direction of atrial activation; compare premature beats across several leads.

front: Which basic laboratory issue should be considered with new frequent atrial ectopy?
back: An electrolyte disturbance.
explanation: Assess illness, losses and medications rather than assuming every premature beat is an isolated primary electrical disorder.

front: Is a PAC an early beat or an escape beat?
back: An early beat.
explanation: An escape beat is a delayed backup impulse after a pause; timing is central to distinguishing them.

front: Which symptoms should prompt renewed assessment in someone known to have PACs?
back: Syncope, exertional symptoms or sustained rapid palpitations.
explanation: Do not let an earlier benign label obscure a new or different cardiac problem.

front: What is the benefit of two-person bag-mask ventilation?
back: One rescuer can maintain a two-handed seal and jaw lift while the other compresses the bag.
explanation: It can improve ventilation when a one-handed seal is inadequate.

front: How can overventilation impair CPR circulation?
back: Excess intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return.
explanation: Avoid excessive rate and volume.

front: What initial rescue-breathing rate is used for an apneic adult with a definite pulse?
back: One breath every 6 seconds, with visible chest rise.
explanation: Reassess pulse and ventilation rather than assuming medication alone will restore breathing.

front: Does oxygen flowing into the bag prove the patient is being ventilated?
back: No. Confirm airway patency, seal and chest rise.
explanation: Obstruction or a leak can prevent effective lung inflation.

front: What is the adult CPR ratio before an advanced airway is placed?
back: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
explanation: Avoid prolonged interruptions for ventilation.

front: What finding makes an oropharyngeal airway poorly tolerated?
back: An intact gag reflex.
explanation: Insertion can provoke gagging or vomiting.

front: Which pharyngeal adjunct may be tolerated when gag reflexes persist?
back: A nasopharyngeal airway, if no contraindication is present.
explanation: Assess trauma and nasal conditions before insertion.

front: Which manual airway maneuver is preferred initially when cervical injury is suspected?
back: Jaw thrust without head extension.
explanation: Airway patency remains the priority while minimizing movement.

front: What does head tilt–chin lift accomplish?
back: It moves the tongue away from the posterior pharynx to improve patency.
explanation: It is used when cervical injury is not suspected.

front: Do oral or nasal pharyngeal airways protect completely against aspiration?
back: No. They do not create a tracheal seal.
explanation: Improved ventilation and airway protection are distinct concepts.

front: What gas-exchange pattern supports bilevel NIV in an appropriate COPD exacerbation?
back: Acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia.
explanation: Clinical suitability and monitoring matter; a blood gas alone is not the complete decision.

references.title: ERS/ATS — noninvasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure

front: How is pressure support calculated on bilevel NIV?
back: IPAP minus EPAP.
explanation: For example, 14/6 cm H2O provides a difference of 8 cm H2O.

references.title: ERS/ATS — noninvasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure

front: Why is active vomiting with impaired airway protection a major problem for NIV?
back: A mask does not protect the trachea from aspiration.
explanation: An invasive airway strategy may be required.

references.title: ERS/ATS — noninvasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure

front: What does worsening acidosis and drowsiness despite NIV suggest?
back: Likely NIV failure requiring urgent reassessment and possible intubation.
explanation: Do not let a prolonged mask trial delay escalation.

references.title: ERS/ATS — noninvasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure

front: Which noninvasive positive-pressure approaches can support selected cardiogenic pulmonary edema patients?
back: CPAP or bilevel NIV.
explanation: Continue treatment of the cause and monitor clinical response.

references.title: ERS/ATS — noninvasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure

front: How does heart rate usually change during inspiration in respiratory sinus arrhythmia?
back: It increases; the R-R interval shortens.
explanation: Expiration usually produces the opposite pattern.

references.title: Children's Hospital of The King's Daughters — sinus arrhythmia

front: What P-wave finding supports a sinus origin despite respiratory irregularity?
back: Consistent sinus P waves before each QRS.
explanation: The rhythm origin remains sinus even though its timing varies.

references.title: Children's Hospital of The King's Daughters — sinus arrhythmia

front: Does asymptomatic physiologic respiratory sinus arrhythmia require an antiarrhythmic?
back: No.
explanation: Treating a normal variant provides no rhythm benefit and adds drug risk.

references.title: Children's Hospital of The King's Daughters — sinus arrhythmia

front: What distinguishes atrial fibrillation from a respiratory sinus rhythm on ECG?
back: Atrial fibrillation lacks consistent organized sinus P waves.
explanation: Irregularity alone is not enough to name the rhythm.

references.title: Children's Hospital of The King's Daughters — sinus arrhythmia

front: Does respiratory sinus arrhythmia exclude a serious cause of exertional syncope?
back: No.
explanation: Assess warning symptoms and family history independently.

references.title: Children's Hospital of The King's Daughters — sinus arrhythmia

front: Which blunt-trauma findings support spinal motion restriction?
back: Midline pain/tenderness or focal neurologic symptoms, among other risk findings.
explanation: Preserved consciousness does not exclude injury.

references.title: American College of Surgeons — Spine Injury Best Practices Guidelines

front: Why does intoxication limit clinical spine clearance?
back: It can make symptom reporting and examination unreliable.
explanation: A negative history alone is insufficient.

references.title: American College of Surgeons — Spine Injury Best Practices Guidelines

front: Is routine immobilization required for every isolated penetrating injury without neurologic signs?
back: No. Do not delay lifesaving care for routine packaging.
explanation: Assess mechanism and findings rather than applying a blanket rule.

references.title: American College of Surgeons — Spine Injury Best Practices Guidelines

front: Should a long backboard remain in place indefinitely after arrival?
back: No. Arrange timely supported transfer when safe.
explanation: An extrication device and ongoing spinal precautions are not the same thing.

references.title: American College of Surgeons — Spine Injury Best Practices Guidelines

front: What takes priority when airway obstruction occurs in suspected cervical injury?
back: Restoring oxygenation while minimizing neck movement.
explanation: Use trained assistance and appropriate airway techniques.

references.title: American College of Surgeons — Spine Injury Best Practices Guidelines

front: Where does a laryngeal mask airway seal?
back: Around the laryngeal inlet, above the vocal cords.
explanation: It is a supraglottic rather than intratracheal device.

references.title: AHA 2025 — advanced airway strategy during CPR

front: What is the immediate purpose of a supraglottic rescue airway after failed intubation?
back: Restore oxygenation and ventilation.
explanation: Definitive planning follows once oxygen delivery is stabilized.

references.title: AHA 2025 — advanced airway strategy during CPR

front: Does successful supraglottic rescue automatically justify continuing an elective procedure?
back: No. Reassess the airway plan and whether to awaken the patient.
explanation: The next step depends on the clinical context and available expertise.

references.title: AHA 2025 — advanced airway strategy during CPR

front: What is required when mask ventilation, supraglottic rescue and intubation all fail to oxygenate?
back: Timely escalation to an emergency invasive-airway pathway.
explanation: Avoid repeated ineffective attempts that prolong hypoxemia.

references.title: AHA 2025 — advanced airway strategy during CPR

front: How should local intubation skill affect advanced-airway choice in cardiac arrest?
back: Use a strategy the team can perform reliably; a supraglottic airway is reasonable with limited intubation proficiency.
explanation: Protect compression quality and verify ventilation.

references.title: AHA 2025 — advanced airway strategy during CPR
